## Claims by unit

### Introduction — Thessalonica, Acts, dating, authorship

**R9-C01** [Intro n.1 | city founding]  
Weima records that Cassander’s wife was named Thessalonike (“Thessalian Victory”) because she was born the day her father Philip II won a battle in Thessaly; she was younger stepsister of Alexander the Great.  
- Quote: “named Thessalonike, which means ‘Thessalian Victory.’ She was the younger stepsister of Alexander the Great.”  
- Pages: `thessalonica`, `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

**R9-C02** [Intro n.5 | free city]  
Evidence of Thessalonica’s “freedom” includes inscription IT 6 and coins inscribed ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΝΙΚΕΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΙΑΣ (“Freedom of the Thessalonians”).  
- Quote: “a series of coins issued by the city inscribed ΘΕΣΣΑΛΟΝΙΚΕΩΝ ΕΛΕΥΘΕΡΙΑΣ (Freedom of the Thessalonians).”  
- Pages: `thessalonica`

**R9-C03** [Intro n.6 | imperial cult protocol]  
Hendrix (via Weima): when “priest and agonothete of the Imperator” is mentioned, he is listed first by protocol, then priest of “the gods,” then priest of Roma and Roman benefactors.  
- Quote: “The Imperator’s priest and agonothete assumes priority, the priest of ‘the gods’ is cited next, followed by the priest of Roma and Roman benefactors.”  
- Pages: `thessalonica`, `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C04** [Intro n.10–11 | politarchs]  
Acts’ πολιτάρχης form is dialectal variation of πολιτάρχος; pre-Roman existence of the office is supported by the gymnasiarchal law of Béroia (Berea) (Gauthier & Hatzopoulos).  
- Quote: “The form πολιτάρχος differs slightly in the suffix (-αρχος instead of -αρχης), which is merely a variation of dialect.”  
- Pages: `thessalonica`, `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C05** [Intro n.19 | Egyptian cults / archaeology]  
Weima uses Perdrizet (1894)—who judged Egyptian cults unimportant in Macedonia from coin silence—as a caution against arguing from silence: after the 1917 fire, a Serapis temple and ultimately sixty-nine inscriptions to Egyptian deities were found, reversing the conclusion.  
- Quote: “a Serapis temple was discovered along with what ultimately numbered sixty-nine inscriptions to various Egyptian deities. … the Egyptian gods were extremely popular in Thessalonica.”  
- Pages: `thessalonica`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

**R9-C06** [Intro n.24 | Acts 17:4 TC]  
Codex Bezae (D) shifts γυναικῶν to nominative γυναῖκες so “wives of the leading men”; with other witnesses adding καί earlier, some read four convert groups: Jews, devout Greeks, pagan Greeks, wives of leading men.  
- Quote: “creates four (rather than three) groups of converts: Jews, Greeks who are ‘devout’ or ‘God-fearers,’ pagan Greeks, and wives of leading men.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `thessalonica`

**R9-C07** [Intro n.26–28 | charges before politarchs]  
Weima (with Schnabel) stresses the first charge’s gravity beyond mild “upset the world” translations; Fitzmyer’s three-charge split fails grammatically (third item is dependent participle on second charge). Fine as penalty was relatively lenient in Roman justice (Keener).  
- Quote: “This charge is much more serious than translations such as ‘these men who have upset the world’ … suggest.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`, `silas`

**R9-C08** [Intro n.30–31 | dating 50–51]  
Timothy’s return (1 Thess 3:6) = Acts 18:5 at Corinth; Gallio proconsulship (Acts 18:12–17) fixed by Delphic Inscription of Claudius to start of one-year term July 51 or 52 → traditional 50–51 for 1 Thessalonians. Literary plural “we” in 3:1–5 helps reconcile Acts itinerary (Donfried).  
- Quote: “an inscription discovered in Delphi … dates the start of Gallio’s one-year term as proconsul to either July 51 or 52.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

**R9-C09** [Intro n.32 | letter order]  
A minority (from Grotius 1640 antichrist discussion through Wanamaker, Trudinger, etc.) reverse 1/2 Thess order; Weima: no a priori bar (sequence may reflect length), but majority find traditional order best.  
- Quote: “the vast majority of scholars have not found the arguments convincing, and the traditional ordering makes the best sense of several issues.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`

**R9-C10** [Intro n.33 | 1 Thess authenticity]  
No serious challenge to Pauline authorship of 1 Thessalonians since the nineteenth century except Crüsemann (2010); earlier Schrader/Baur line was quickly refuted. Fee: denial faces “enormous historical difficulties—so much so that one wonders, ‘Why bother?’”  
- Quote: “over a century of scholarship has now passed without any significant challenge to Paul’s authorship of 1 Thessalonians.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C11** [Intro n.39–41 | 2 Thess authenticity]  
Weima (Malherbe, Foster): majority still affirm genuineness; Foster’s BNTC 2011 survey (109 respondents): 63 yes / 13 no / 35 uncertain Paul authored 2 Thessalonians. Jewett: post-Trilling 1972 visible shift against authenticity. The four classic anti-authenticity arguments already summarized by Hollmann (1904).  
- Quote: “Of the 109 respondents … 63 answered ‘yes’ … 13 answered ‘no,’ and 35 answered ‘uncertain.’”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `2-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C12** [Intro n.42 | tone difference]  
Malherbe: readers of 2 Thess had recently read 1 Thess; Paul could assume positive relationship (1 Thess 3:6–9) and need not repeat the same relational cultivation—mitigating “colder tone” arguments.  
- Quote: “the readers of 2 Thessalonians had also read 1 Thessalonians not too long before. … there was no need to repeat his earlier effort to that end.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians-authorship`

### 1 Thessalonians 1:1–10 (opening / thanksgiving)

**R9-C13** [1:1 n.3–4 | Christology]  
Double object God + Christ with single ἐν only at 1 Thess 1:1 and 2 Thess 1:1; double object with ἀπό appears in other Pauline greetings. Morris: κύριος works for Jewish or pagan readers as divine claim.  
- Quote: “The only other occurrence of the double object of God and Christ with the single preposition ἐν is 2 Thess. 1:1.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`

**R9-C14** [1:2–10 n.3 | thanksgiving form]  
Weima schematizes Schubert’s Type 1a (complex: Phil, Col, 1 Thess, Phlm — principal + participial + purpose) vs Type 1b (simple: 1 Cor, 2 Thess — principal + ὅτι + ὥστε).  
- Quote: “Type 1b: Simple (1 Corinthians; 2 Thessalonians) … Causal Clause: introduced by ὅτι … Consecutive Clause: introduced by ὥστε.”  
- Pages: `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`

**R9-C15** [1:2–10 n.12, 19–20 | triad / election]  
Faith–love–hope triad first in Paul; no need to posit pre-Pauline apostolic compendium (contra Hunter); Malherbe: order varies with emphasis last. Election (1:4) responds to suffering (Donfried/Fee) and functions as “language of belonging” vs pagan cults (Wanamaker).  
- Quote: “the belief of the Thessalonians in their election by God was of tremendous social significance, since … it gave them a new identity … [and] helped symbolically to annihilate the world of their previous social existence.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `concepts` (election / faith-hope-love as relevant)

**R9-C16** [1:2–10 n.25, 46 | Spirit / idols / God-fearers]  
Anarthrous πνεῦμα ἅγιον still = personal Holy Spirit (Paul often drops article in prep. phrases). “Turned from idols” marks primarily Gentile church; God-fearers could still participate in pagan cults (Fredriksen; Levinskaya), so no necessary conflict with Acts 17 synagogue converts.  
- Quote: “Some of the God-fearers were only one step from becoming converts, while others just added the Jewish God to their pantheon.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `thessalonica`

### 1 Thessalonians 2:1–16 (+ Excursus 2: νήπιοι)

**R9-C17** [2:1–16 n.2–5, 9 | apologia function]  
Older label: 2:1–16 *apologia pro vita sua*; primary function defensive (actual or potential charges), not merely paraenetic modeling; attack targets integrity not apostolic status (outsider opponents vs Galatians insiders).  
- Quote: “in either situation, the function of 2:1–16 remains the same: Paul … is attempting to defend himself and so reestablish the trust and confidence of his readers.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C18** [2:1–16 n.12 | Philippi suffering verbs]  
Rejecting Acts 16 leads Richard to minimize suffering in 2:2 (active “fight” for προπάσχω; verbal-only “insult” for ὑβρίζω); majority take passive suffering and physical punishment.  
- Quote: “Richard opts for a rarer active sense of ‘to fight or struggle.’ … Richard restricts its meaning to verbal abuse.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`

**R9-C19** [Excursus 2 n.3–4, 6 | TC 2:7 νήπιοι vs ἤπιοι]  
NA26+ and UBS4 favor νήπιοι (“infants”) over ἤπιοι (“gentle”)—UBS B-rating “almost certain.” External weight: 𝔓65, א*, B, D*, Old Latin, versions/Fathers (Metzger). Sailors TLG: νήπιος ~7× more common than ἤπιος in 1st c. BC–AD; Weima DDBDP ~1:3. Translations almost all still print “gentle” (exceptions TNIV/NIV/NET).  
- Quote: “The weight and diversity of external evidence are clearly in favour of νήπιοι.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

**R9-C20** [2:1–16 n.54, 56 | Jewish opposition aorist / Acts]  
Aorist participle (2:15) marks simple/specific action (Aktionsart), not past-only time; supports a discrete expulsion like Acts 17:5 rather than generic ongoing Jewish hostility. Malherbe: only extreme skepticism about Acts + interpolation theory of 2:13–16 blocks this reading.  
- Quote: “the aorist participle supports a specific act of Jewish opposition such as is described in Acts 17:5.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`

**R9-C21** [2:1–16 n.58–59 | 2:16c wrath / εἰς τέλος]  
Near-identical ἔφθασεν … ἡ ὀργὴ … εἰς τέλος in T. Levi 6.11—whether Christian interpolation from Paul or shared Jewish judgment formula remains unsettled and does not fix the historical referent of 2:16. Frame’s parallelism of 2:16b (πάντοτε) // 2:16c (εἰς τέλος) requires temporal sense for εἰς τέλος.  
- Quote: “the relationship of T. Levi 6.11 to 1 Thess. 2.16 is still unsettled and cannot resolve the meaning of the words in our passage.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

### 1 Thessalonians 2:17–3:13

**R9-C22** [2:17–3:10 n.3–5, 9 | apostolic parousia]  
Funk’s “apostolic parousia” ≠ mere “travelogue”: presence via future visit, emissary, or letter. 2:17–3:10 labeled *apologia pro absentia sua*. Mitchell: envoy sometimes more effective than Paul’s own visit.  
- Quote: “the latter term refers more comprehensively to the presence of Paul, whether … a future visit … the arrival of his emissary, or the letter itself.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`, `timothy`

**R9-C23** [2:17–3:10 n.14, 17 | orphan / literary “we”]  
Orphan metaphor + passive “separated” + “who drove us out” (2:15) support forced flight (Acts 17:10). Singulars “I, Paul” (2:18; 3:5; 5:27) show Paul is real author; plurals = literary.  
- Quote: “Paul rather than all three missionaries is the real author of the letter; the plural ‘we’ … ought also to be interpreted as a literary plural, not as literal.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `paul`, `silas`, `timothy`

**R9-C24** [2:17–3:10 n.27, 39 | στέγω / ἄρτι]  
Weima re-reads στέγω via “roof/keep in-out” image (not only “endure”): 1 Cor 9:12 rights “kept in”; 1 Cor 13:7 love “covers” negatives—so 3:1 “no longer able to ‘contain’ [the separation].” ἄρτι at 3:6 = general “now” (Pauline pattern), not “just this moment” after Timothy’s return.  
- Quote: “although Paul no doubt wrote … soon after the coming of Timothy, it does not appear that he is here emphasizing that he sent his letter immediately upon the return of his envoy.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

### 1 Thessalonians 4:1–12 (sexual ethics / idleness)

**R9-C25** [4:1–12 n.24–25 | σκεῦος]  
4:4 is “almost certainly the most debated text in the whole letter” (20+ articles + dissertation). Weima: masculine pronouns + σκεῦος as male sex organ → address primarily males; evidence that σκεῦος = both sexes’ genitals is weak.  
- Quote: “the likelihood that σκεῦος refers to the male sex organ suggest that Paul is addressing primarily the male members of the Thessalonian church.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C26** [4:1–12 n.28–29 | πρᾶγμα / situation]  
Baltensweiler’s ἐπίκληρος/heiress-lawsuit theory for πρᾶγμα fails (Best lists six difficulties; virtually no support). Fee’s “best answer overall”: at least one adulterous case (another man’s wife or household slave).  
- Quote: “at least one case of sexual sin has been an adulterous situation with another man’s wife, or perhaps with a household slave.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C27** [4:1–12 n.35–37 | θεοδίδακτοι / covenant]  
θεοδίδακτος nearly unique to 1 Thess 4:9 (later Christian cites of this verse; one 11th-c. non-Christian use). Deidun: Jer 31:34 + Ezek 37:14 (36:27) evoke covenant/messianic immediacy of God’s teaching.  
- Quote: “By utilizing the parallel texts of Jeremiah and Ezekiel in I Thess. 4,8b–9, Paul wishes to recall to the Thessalonians their unique Covenant relationship with God.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C28** [4:1–12 n.10, 41 | idleness trajectory 1→2 Thess]  
1 Thess appeals (4:10b–12; 5:14); 2 Thess escalates to extended “command” (3:6–15) as problem worsened. Dense lexical parallels (ἡσυχάζειν/ἡσυχία, ἐργάζεσθαι, παραγγέλλω, ἀτακτ- root, busybodies) lead Russell: “2 Thess 3.6–13 is a commentary on 1 Thess 4.11–12 and 5.14.” Weima defends using 2 Thess to illuminate 1 Thess on authenticity grounds.  
- Quote: “These parallels lead Russell (1988: 114n10) to conclude that ‘2 Thess 3.6–13 is a commentary on 1 Thess 4.11–12 and 5.14.’”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`

### 1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11 (parousia comfort)

**R9-C29** [4:13–18 n.5, 14–15 | logic / anti-rapture]  
Paul omits a step: resurrection + ascent needed to link Jesus’s death/resurrection to deceased sharing the parousia (Nicholl). Transformation of living not taught here (drawn from 1 Cor 15; Phil 3:21). Fee: secret rapture cannot be intended—Thessalonians had no prior instruction of such an event “otherwise unknown in the church until the mid-nineteenth century.”  
- Quote: “so how could they have known about such an ‘event’ otherwise unknown in the church until the mid-nineteenth century?”  
- Pages: `parousia-1-thess-4`, `1-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C30** [4:13–18 n.11, 16–17 | κέλευσμα / ἁρπάζω / ἀπάντησις]  
Luckensmeyer: possible counter-imperial use of κέλευσμα vs imperial κέλευσις. Malherbe: ἁρπάζω “neat twist”—usually separation from living, here snatching into association with Lord/Christians. Debate on εἰς ἀπάντησιν: Sinai theophany (Dupont) vs Hellenistic formal receptions; Luckensmeyer: not strict technical term, but Hellenistic reception influence “cannot be rejected.” Chrysostom: as when a king arrives, honored go out to meet; condemned wait within.  
- Quote: “an association of Paul’s reference with Hellenistic formal receptions cannot be rejected.”  
- Pages: `parousia-1-thess-4`, `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C31** [5:1–11 n.3, 5 | day of the Lord / “peace and security”]  
Fee/Shogren: transferring OT “day of the LORD” to Jesus’s coming is high Christology / indirect affirmation of deity already in earliest letter. Malherbe’s “false prophets inside” reading of “peace and security” (5:3) rejected—contrast throughout is with outsiders.  
- Quote: “all of the ‘day’ references are therefore indirect but unmistakable affirmations of Christ’s deity.”  
- Pages: `parousia-1-thess-4`, `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C32** [5:1–11 n.22–24 | “asleep” in 5:10]  
εἴτε γρηγορῶμεν εἴτε καθεύδωμεν = death/life, not moral vigilance alone; Luckensmeyer (even while preferring vigilance metaphor elsewhere) concedes καθεύδειν *can* mean death. ἅμα = association of believers with one another, not with Christ (that is “with him”).  
- Quote: “the ridiculous claim that καθεύδειν is rarely or never used to refer to death, needs to be put away once and for all.”  
- Pages: `parousia-1-thess-4`, `1-thessalonians`

### 1 Thessalonians 5:12–28

**R9-C33** [5:12–22 n.11–13 | ἄτακτοι]  
Not general “sinners” (contra Chrysostom’s broad take) but “rebellious idlers”—idleness + disorder combined; NIV 2011 “idle and disruptive” risks sounding like two groups.  
- Quote: “Paul rebukes both the sin of idleness and rebelliousness—two sins that happen to be combined in the lives of some members.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians`

**R9-C34** [5:23–28 n.10–11 | spirit/soul/body]  
Weima surveys trichotomy theories (Dobschütz divine πνεῦμα; Masson; Stempvoort; Jewett gnostic enthusiasts; Dibelius traditional formula; Marshall aspects not parts) and sides with completeness of sanctification; Fee stresses inclusion of the body for a Gentile church.  
- Quote: “Paul is concerned that this early, almost totally Gentile … congregation understand that salvation in Christ includes the sanctification of the body.”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C35** [5:23–28 n.19–20 | holy kiss]  
Early problems: erotic risk / pagan suspicion—Tertullian (pagan husband bars wife from kiss); Athenagoras (second kiss for pleasure sins); Clement (foul suspicions). Later Eastern practice: ask during kiss whether anyone harbors anger (Dix).  
- Quote: “a pagan husband would not allow his wife ‘to meet any one of the brethren to exchange the kiss’ (Ux. 2.4).”  
- Pages: `1-thessalonians`

### 2 Thessalonians 1 (opening / thanksgiving)

**R9-C36** [2 Thess 1:1–2 n.4 | peace as letter goal?]  
Bassler’s “inclusio of peace” (1:2 // 3:16) making peace the theological goal is rejected: 1:2 is formulaic; εἰρήνη never appears in letter body; appeals to ἄνεσις (1:7) and ἡσυχία (3:12) do not suffice.  
- Quote: “The evidence, therefore, does not justify defining peace as the theological goal of the letter.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

**R9-C37** [2 Thess 1:3–12 n.2, 9, 13 | consolation / retribution]  
Thanksgiving’s consolatory purpose often under-read (Malherbe; some older Germans/French). “Theology of suffering” reading of 1:5 (affliction as evidence that makes worthy) has recent English uptake (Bassler, Wanamaker, Menken, Gaventa, Green, Nicholl, etc.). Shift in 1:7b–10: retribution subject becomes “the Lord Jesus,” bearing God’s name/functions (Menken; Marshall).  
- Quote: “now ‘the Lord Jesus’ is the subject of the retribution. … he bears God’s own name and exercises God’s functions, among them the office of eschatological judge.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `parousia-1-thess-4`

**R9-C38** [2 Thess 1:3–12 n.17, 23 | vengeance / “God” of Jesus]  
Nicholl: 8b–9 is generic (not feeding hunger for vengeance on specific persecutors—that was v. 6). Dobschütz took 1:12b ascription of “God” to Jesus as non-Pauline interpolation—no MS support; Weima notes other NT ascriptions and possible Rom 9:5.  
- Quote: “the biggest weakness to Dobschütz’s hypothesis of interpolation is that it has absolutely no textual support.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`

### 2 Thessalonians 2 (day of the Lord, lawless one, restrainer)

**R9-C39** [2:1–17 n.2–4 | pastoral priority]  
Giblin: apocalyptic subordinated to pastoral correction. Fee et al.: ch. 2 is primary occasion of letter; suffering (ch. 1) and idle (ch. 3) often related to day-of-the-Lord confusion. Weima rejects downplaying the crisis as non-serious (contra Moore, Shogren).  
- Quote: “Paul seems to be more concerned with the pastoral problem of correcting the Thessalonians’ outlook than he is with describing the coming of the Antichrist.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `antichrist`, `parousia-1-thess-4`

**R9-C40** [2:1–17 n.14–16 | ellipsis / ἀποστασία ≠ rapture]  
Incomplete conditional (ellipsis, not illogical anacoluthon) makes pseudonymous forger less likely (Wanamaker: forger would carefully fill a key point). English/Wuest/House “departure/rapture” reading of ἀποστασία implausible: noun means religious apostasy/political rebellion in LXX–NT, never positive rapture, and is paired with man of lawlessness.  
- Quote: “the noun ἀποστασία in the LXX, intertestamental literature, and NT has the special sense of religious ‘apostasy’ or political and military ‘rebellion’ and never the nuance of ‘departure.’”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `antichrist`, `parousia-1-thess-4`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`

**R9-C41** [2:1–17 n.18, 20, 23–24 | temple / prior teaching / mystery]  
ὥστε + infinitive in Koine need not mean only “intended” result—man of lawlessness’ seating expresses height of rebellion whether actual or intended. Imperfect ἔλεγον (2:5) implies repeated eschatological teaching → mission longer than three Sabbaths. Beale: “mystery” + Daniel allusion = enigmatic present fulfillment; if restrainer = Michael (Dan 10–12), strengthens Beale. ἐνεργεῖται middle or passive—either way within God’s plan (Malherbe).  
- Quote: “Paul’s mission-founding ministry in Thessalonica lasted longer than three Sabbaths.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `antichrist`, `thessalonica`

**R9-C42** [Excursus 3 n.1–4 + 2:6–7 notes | restrainer]  
τὸ κατέχον lacks object; αὐτόν already anticipated. Survey omits fringe views; combinations exist (Hendriksen, Ford, Beale). Krodel objection to all ID theories: why use κατέχον not “emperor/governor/apostle/angel/God”? Hannah: Paul prefers abstract power language over explicit “angel.” Weima links Rev 20:2 binding of Satan to present-age restraint parallel to 2:7 (amillennial present reign reading).  
- Quote: “They are unable to explain why the author … used the word katechon (-ōn) instead of emperor, or governor, or apostle, or angel, or God.”  
- Pages: `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`

**R9-C43** [2:1–17 n.29, 37 | focus on Christ not Antichrist]  
Holmes/Best/Fee: minimal necessary knowledge of the Rebel; gaze stays on the Lord—not Left Behind–style Antichrist fascination. 2:11–12 rhetoric comforts under persecution (Wanamaker; Fee), not primarily threatens Thessalonians.  
- Quote: “When novels about Antichrist … outsell books about Jesus, it seems to me that there is something seriously out of balance.”  
- Pages: `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`, `restrainer-2-thess-2`

**R9-C44** [2:1–17 n.44, 53, 55 | Trinity / letter reference / Christology]  
2:13 joins God, Lord (Jesus), Spirit in one verse (Fee proto-Trinitarian list). 2:15 “letter” = prior letter (1 Thess), not present 2 Thess—would need article as in 3:14; 5:27 pattern. Prayer 2:16 high Christology assumed not argued (Fee; Shogren).  
- Quote: “if Paul had wanted to refer to the present letter, he would have used the definite article … as he does in the following chapter (3:14).”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `1-thessalonians`

### 2 Thessalonians 3 (idlers / closing)

**R9-C45** [3:1–15 n.1–2, 18, 28, 35–36 | structure & idleness]  
Unit 3:1–15 (not to 3:16 peace benediction = closing header; not ending at 3:12). Ch. 2 primary problem; idlers not “saved for last” as most important (contra Fee overstatement). “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” = theological coercion: disobedience to Lord not only Paul (Wanamaker). Wordplay 3:11 ἐργαζομένους/περιεργαζομένους; Green’s patron-client public-assembly theory overconfident. ἄτακτοι not free-time preachers (Nicholl).  
- Quote: “the addition of ‘in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ’ to a command implies that the command is not simply Paul’s but that it has the sanction of the Lord Jesus Christ himself.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `1-thessalonians`

**R9-C46** [3:16–18 n.4–6 | autograph]  
Shift to singular “I, Paul” (also 2:5) confirms literary plurals. Autograph authenticates and authorizes (Marshall; Holmes; Wanamaker)—not only anti-forgery. Secular papyri: senders usually closed in own hand without saying so (Deissmann; Weima *Neglected Endings*).  
- Quote: “Paul’s purpose is to emphasize the authority and authenticity of this letter rather than to deny the authenticity of other alleged letters of his.”  
- Pages: `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `jeffrey-weima`, `paul`
